working: The line opens with the C3 clef and three sharps, with no time signature. That means it continues a passage. First stretch, up to the first barline: five repeated notes at the same pitch under one beam. They read as E4 16th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 16th. That is the end of bar 70, after its slurred 16ths and D#4 8ths, which must be on the line before. So the line begins partway through bar 70. Second stretch, between the two barlines: groups of four 32nds. One lower group (E4), two higher groups (eight A4s), one lower group (F#4). Then comes a long group of sixteen 32nds under heavy beams, at a higher pitch. That is bar 71, with the edition's two B4 tremolo quarters written out as 32nds. Third stretch, after the second barline: four groups of four 32nds, all on one pitch. That is the sixteen E4 32nds that open bar 72. After them is a wavy sign and no barline. This is probably a custos, or possibly a sign for repeating the figure. It stands for, or leads into, the rest of bar 72 (the two E4 tremolo quarters). So the line ends inside bar 72. Nothing in the line matches bar 69 or bar 73.
insights: The 32nd groups and the two barlines make bars 71 and 72 easy to match. The opening run of repeated E4s is short, but it can only be the end of bar 70. The open ending was the harder part: a wavy sign with no barline, and the tremolo quarters either written out or left off. A view of the next line's opening would settle whether the rest of bar 72 is there.

working:
Start: clef and the three-sharp key signature. Then five beamed notes, all on the same pitch (E4). These match the last five notes of bar 70: E4 16th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 8th, E4 16th. So the line takes over bar 70 partway through, after the D#4 8ths that ended the previous line.

After the first barline come eight groups of four 32nds. The first four groups are lower: E4 ×4, A4 ×4, A4 ×4, F#4 ×4, which is the first half of bar 71. The next four groups sit higher, under one heavy shared beam. They are the B4 notes that the edition prints as two quarter-note tremolos, written out here as 16 32nds. That is the whole of bar 71.

After the second barline come four more groups of four 32nds, all on one repeated pitch. They match the opening of bar 72: 16 E4 32nds. The line ends with a wavy custos (a mark showing the next line's first note). Bar 72's two E4 quarter tremolos are missing, so the next line must finish that bar.

So the line holds bars 70 (end), 71 (whole) and 72 (start). The program stops at bar 71 and misses the start of bar 72.
insights: The copyist writes out the edition's tremolos as plain 32nd groups. Their dense beams make the beat count and the repeated pitches hard to read. The last measure has no closing barline and ends in a custos, so the partial bar 72 is easy to overlook. Counting beats per barline (32 32nds per bar) against the edition, and seeing the start of the next line, would have settled it quickly.

working: Clef C3, three sharps. 1) Before the first barline there are four beamed groups of four 32nds on one low note (A3). That is 16 32nds, half a bar. Bar 85 is a dotted-quarter rest plus 20 A3 32nds (five groups). So the rests and the first group must be at the end of the line before, and this line starts partway into bar 85. Its last four groups are here. 2) Between the first and second barlines there are eight groups of four 32nds. That makes 32 32nds, one full 4/4 bar, with the repeated notes written out instead of as tremolos. The first group sits lower (A3) and the other seven higher (A4). This matches bar 86: A3, then A4 ×3, as quarter tremolos. 'cresc.' is written under the middle of the bar; the edition's text gives no dynamics. 3) After the second barline, with 'f:' under it, there are four groups of four 32nds on A4. That is 16 32nds, half of bar 87 (four A4 quarter tremolos). The line ends there, partway through bar 87, and the next line finishes the bar. Nothing contradicts the edition. Bar 88's drop to E4 does not appear on this line.
insights: The copyist writes out the tremolos as beamed 32nd groups. That means counting groups: eight per full bar, four per half bar. The counts show the line both starts and ends partway through a bar, which the barlines alone don't reveal. The bars are all repeated notes, so they are told apart mainly by rhythm and the A3/A4 register change. Showing the end of the previous line, so the bar-85 rests are visible, would have settled where the line starts.
